title: 論語 雍也第六
source: Confucius 孔子 and his disciples, 論語 (the Analects), book 6, 〈雍也〉, in the received text as printed in Zhu Xi 朱熹, 論語集注 (part of his 四書章句集注, completed c. 1190), from the Wenyuange 文淵閣 copy of the Siku Quanshu 四庫全書 (1782), as transcribed by the Kanseki Repository (Kanripo, KR1h0015). Collated character by character against two further pre-1930 printings, both transcribed by Kanripo: Ruan Yuan's 1816 Nanchang reprint of the Song edition of 論語注疏 (KR1h0004) and He Yan's 論語集解 in the Sibu Congkan photographic reprint of a Song edition (KR1h0005). Readings that change the sense are noted in the notes; graphic variants (悌 for 弟, 爲 for 為) are not. Zhu Xi's text is substantially the one James Legge printed in The Chinese Classics, vol. 1 (Hong Kong, 1861), and the passage numbering is the standard one. All punctuation is editorial — the original has none. Characters are traditional, as the edition prints them (衆, not 眾). Translations are made fresh from the Chinese. Pronunciation convention: modern Mandarin, given in Hanyu Pinyin — an admitted anachronism, and the living convention for reading these texts. Any prepared audio is synthesized speech in that same modern Mandarin convention; the exact voice used is recorded in audio/<id>/voice.txt and is fixed for every Chinese text.
about: Book 6 of the Analects, 雍也 Yōng yě, named, as every book is, from its first words ("Yong…", the personal name of the disciple Ran Yong). The Analects is a collection of short sayings and exchanges of Confucius (Kǒngzǐ, 551–479 BC) and his disciples, put together by their followers over several generations; the twenty books were not composed as a whole, and nothing in them was written down by Confucius himself. Zhu Xi notes that the first half of this book goes on as Book 5 did, weighing people: Ran Yong fit to face south as a ruler (6.1), Yan Hui the one disciple who truly loved learning, dead young (6.2), and never straying from humaneness for three months together (6.5), content in a poor lane with a basket of rice and a gourd of water (6.9); the Master grieving at the bedside of the sick Bo Niu (6.8), and telling Ran Qiu that he has drawn his own line before his strength ran out (6.10). The second half gathers some of the most quoted sayings in the book: plain stuff and pattern in balance (6.16), knowing a thing, loving it and delighting in it (6.18), the wise delighting in water and the humane in mountains (6.21), the gu vessel that is no longer a gu (6.23), the Master's visit to Nanzi, the notorious wife of the ruler of Wei, and his oath to the offended Zilu (6.26), the virtue of the constant mean (6.27), and to close, what humaneness is: wishing to stand oneself, setting others up (6.28). Each numbered passage (6.1–6.28, Zhu Xi's chapters) begins a new card; longer passages are cut where Zhu Xi's commentary interrupts the text. In 6.28 the edition we follow misprints 已 and 巳 for 己 'oneself'; the reading text is corrected and the note says so. The original has no punctuation: every comma, quotation mark and full stop is an editor's interpretation. Read the characters; the pinyin under each one is a reading aid you can hide with the transcription button.

sentences.t: 子曰：「雍也可使南面。」
sentences.l: The Master said: “Yong — he could be made to face south.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “Yong could be set on a ruler's seat.”
sentences.n: The book is named 雍也 from its first words, 'Yong…'. Zhu Xi heads it: twenty-eight chapters in all, and up to the fourteenth the drift is the same as the book before — weighing men, past and present. 雍 Yong is Ran Yong 冉雍, courtesy name Zhonggong 仲弓, of 5.4. 南面 'to face south': the ruler sat facing south to hear the business of government (Zhu Xi: 人君聽治之位), so to 'face south' is to rule. Zhu Xi: the Master means that Zhonggong was broad, generous, plain and weighty (寬洪簡重) and had the measure of a ruler. He Yan's Bao Xian narrows it: he could be entrusted with a feudal state and govern it. Variant: He Yan's text ends 可使南面也.

sentences.t:
仲弓問子桑伯子。
子曰：「可也，簡。」

words.reading: 子桑伯子 zǐ sāng bó zǐ

morph.gloss: Zisang Bozi — a man of Lu

sentences.l:
Zhonggong asked about Zisang Bozi.
The Master said: “He will do —
he is easy.”
sentences.i: Zhonggong asked about Zisang Bozi. The Master said: “He passes. He does not make a fuss over things.”
sentences.n: 子桑伯子 Zisang Bozi, Zhu Xi says, was a man of Lu; he records Hu Yin's guess that he is the 子桑戶 Zisang Hu of the Zhuangzi. He Yan's Wang Su: nothing is known of him from the books and records. Zhu Xi: because the Master had granted that Zhonggong could face south, he asked how Bozi measured up. 可 is only 'passable' — Zhu Xi: 僅可而有所未盡之辭, a word for 'barely enough, with something still lacking'. 簡 is 'not troublesome' (不煩之謂): easy, unfussy, sparing of rules. He Yan's commentary takes it the other way: 'he is passable, because he can be simple'.

sentences.t:
仲弓曰：「
居敬而行簡，
以臨其民，
不亦可乎？
居簡而行簡，
無乃大簡乎？」

morph.gloss: Zhong, the courtesy name of Guan Yiwu

sentences.l:
Zhonggong said: “Abiding in reverence and acting with ease,
and so presiding over one's people —
is that not acceptable indeed?
Abiding in ease and acting with ease —
is that not rather too easy?”
sentences.i: Zhonggong said: “To hold oneself in reverence and keep things simple in dealing with others as one rules the people — surely that will do. But to be easy in oneself and easy in one's dealings too — is that not taking ease too far?”
sentences.n: 居 'to abide, to hold oneself'; 行 'to act' (xíng), here in one's dealings with the people; 臨 'to look down on', the word for a ruler facing those below. 不亦…乎 'is it not indeed…?' (1.1). 無乃…乎 is a fixed form, 'is it not rather…?', putting a doubt mildly. 大 is read tài, 'too much' (Zhu Xi: 大音泰). Zhu Xi: if one holds oneself in reverence, there is a master within and one governs oneself strictly; then to act simply in ruling the people means affairs are not troublesome and the people are not harassed — that is acceptable. If one first holds oneself loosely, there is no master within and self-government is slack, and if one's dealings are loose too, is that not too loose, leaving no law to keep? He adds that the Kongzi jiayu records Bozi going about without cap or robe, and the Master faulting him for wanting to make the human way the same as an ox's or a horse's — so Bozi was the 'too easy' kind, and Zhonggong suspected the Master of praising him too readily. He Yan's Kong Anguo: holding oneself reverent and grave while being lenient and simple towards those below is acceptable. Variant: He Yan's text writes 太簡, the same word.

sentences.t: 子曰：「雍之言然。」
sentences.l: The Master said: “Yong's words are right.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “Yong is right.”
sentences.n: 然 'so, thus', here 'it is so, you are right'. Zhu Xi: Zhonggong had probably not grasped what the Master meant by 'he will do', but the principle he stated tacitly matched it, so the Master agreed. He quotes Master Cheng: Bozi's ease had something to commend it but was not wholly good, hence 'he will do'; Zhonggong then said that reverence as the master within with simplicity in action is the essential, while simplicity within as well as without is mere slackness — he caught the point; and again: abide in reverence and the heart holds nothing, so one's acts are simple of themselves; abide in ease and one has first set the heart on being easy, which is one 'easy' too many — hence 'too easy'.

sentences.t:
哀公問：「
弟子孰為好學？」
孔子對曰：「
有顏回者好學，
不遷怒，
不貳過。
不幸短命死矣！
今也則亡，
未聞好學者也。」

morph.gloss: Duke Ai — the ruler of Lu
deference to elders, a younger brother's duty (later written 悌)
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
Duke Ai asked: “Of your disciples, who is fond of learning?”
Kongzi answered, saying: “There was Yan Hui, who was fond of learning:
he did not shift his anger,
he did not repeat a fault.
Unluckily he was short-lived, and he has died.
Now there is none;
I have not heard of one fond of learning.”
sentences.i: Duke Ai asked which of the disciples loved learning. Kongzi answered: “There was Yan Hui. He loved learning. His anger never strayed onto someone who had not earned it, and a fault once made he never made again. Sadly he was not given long, and he is dead. Now there is no one — I have not heard of anyone else who loves learning.”
sentences.n: 哀公 is Duke Ai of Lu (2.19); because a ruler asks, the book writes 孔子對曰, with the formal 對. 孰 'who, which'; 為 wéi 'is'; 好 hào 'to be fond of' (Zhu Xi: 去聲). 顏回 Yan Hui is Yan Yuan (5.8, 5.25). 遷 is 'to move', 貳 'to repeat' (Zhu Xi: 遷移也，貳復也): anger at one man is not moved onto another, a fault made once is not made again — Zhu Xi calls it the fruit of Yan Hui's 'overcoming himself' (克己). 短命 'short of allotted life': Zhu Xi says he died at thirty-two (others count otherwise). 亡 is wú, the same word as 無 'there is none' (Zhu Xi: 亡與無同). Saying 'now there is none' and then 'I have not heard of one', Zhu Xi says, shows how deeply the Master grieved, and how hard a real lover of learning is to find. He quotes Master Cheng at length: Yan Hui's anger lay in the thing, not in himself, so it did not shift; when anything in him was not good he always knew it, and knowing it never did it again; and, asked what learning Yan Hui loved, when the other seventy disciples all knew the Odes, the Documents and the six arts: learning by which one reaches the Way of the sage. He Yan's commentary: most men give way to feeling and their anger goes against reason; Yan Yuan followed the Way, and his anger did not go past its measure. Variant: He Yan's text reads 哀公問曰.

sentences.t:
子華使於齊，
冉子為其母請粟。
子曰：「與之釡。」
請益。
曰：「與之庾。」
冉子與之粟五秉。

morph.gloss: a fu (= 釜, a measure of grain)
Ran, a surname (Ran You, Ran Qiu)
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
Zihua was sent on a mission to Qi,
and Master Ran asked grain for his mother.
The Master said: “Give her a fu.”
He asked for more.
He said: “Give her a yu.”
Master Ran gave her five bing of grain.
sentences.i: When Zihua was away on a mission to Qi, Master Ran asked for an allowance of grain for his mother. The Master said: “Give her a fu.” Ran asked for more. “Give her a yu, then.” Ran gave her five bing.
sentences.n: 子華 Zihua is Gongxi Chi 公西赤 (5.7). 使 Zhu Xi reads shì, 'to go as envoy' (使為並去聲), and says Zihua went on the Master's own business; modern practice reads shǐ, and we give shǐ. 冉子 'Master Ran' is Ran Qiu 冉求 (Zhu Xi quotes Master Cheng calling him 求; He Yan's Zheng Xuan calls him 冉有); 為其母 'for his mother', 為 wèi (Zhu Xi: 去聲). 粟 is unhusked grain. The three measures, as Zhu Xi gives them: a 釡 fu (the edition's form of 釜) is six dou and four sheng, a 庾 yu sixteen dou, a 秉 bing sixteen hu (a hu is ten dou) — so five bing is eighty hu, more than a hundred times the first offer; He Yan's Ma Rong and Bao Xian give the same figures. 益 'more'. Ran Qiu, that is, ignored both answers.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
赤之適齊也，
乘肥馬，
衣輕裘。
吾聞之也：
君子周急不繼富。」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
The Master said: “Chi, going to Qi,
rode well-fed horses,
wore light furs.
I have heard it said:
the gentleman makes up for the needy, and does not add to the rich.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “When Chi set off for Qi he had sleek horses to draw him and fine light furs on his back. I have heard that a gentleman helps those who are in want; he does not top up those who have plenty.”
sentences.n: 赤之適齊也 'Chi's going to Qi': 之 makes the clause a topic, and 適 is shì 'to go to'. 乘 is chéng 'to ride, drive', 衣 is yì 'to wear' (Zhu Xi: 衣去聲); fat horses and light furs, Zhu Xi says, show that he was rich. 急 is 'hard-pressed, in want' (窮迫); Zhu Xi: 周 is to make up what is lacking, 繼 to add to what is already over. He quotes Master Cheng: the Master's sending Zihua, and Zihua's going on his errand, were right; Ran Qiu asked on his behalf, and the sage, broad and tolerant, did not like to refuse a man outright, so he offered little, to show that nothing was owed, and when asked for more again offered little, to show that more was not owed; Qiu did not see it and gave much on his own, which was going too far — so the Master faulted him; had Chi truly been in want the Master would have helped him himself, without waiting to be asked. He Yan's Zheng Xuan: the Master is faulting Ran You for giving too much.

sentences.t:
原思為之宰，
與之粟九百，
辭。

morph.gloss: Yuan Si — Yuan Xian, a disciple

sentences.i: Yuan Si was the Master's steward. He was given nine hundred measures of grain, and he declined it.
sentences.n: 原思 Yuan Si is the disciple Yuan Xian 原憲 (Zhu Xi), courtesy name Zisi 子思 (He Yan's Bao Xian: 思字也). 為之宰 'acted as his steward', 為 wéi: Zhu Xi says that when Confucius was Minister of Crime (司寇) in Lu he made Si steward of his household; Bao Xian says of his household's town. The grain is the steward's salary (Zhu Xi: 宰之祿也). 'Nine hundred' gives no measure, and Zhu Xi says it cannot now be known; He Yan's Kong Anguo takes it as nine hundred dou. 辭 'to decline' (Kong Anguo: 辭讓不受, he declined and would not accept).

sentences.t:
子曰：「毋！
以與爾鄰里鄉黨乎！」
sentences.l:
The Master said: “Do not!
Give it to your neighbours and village, your district and ward!”
sentences.i: The Master said: “Do not refuse it! Take it and give it to your neighbours, to the people of your village and district.”
sentences.n: 毋 wú 'do not' forbids (Zhu Xi: 禁止辭). 以與 'take it and give'. The four words are units of the Zhou countryside, as Zhu Xi (and He Yan's Zheng Xuan) gives them: five households make a 鄰, twenty-five a 里, twelve thousand five hundred a 鄉, five hundred a 黨 — together, all the people about him. Zhu Xi: a regular salary should not be declined; whatever is over can be passed on to help the poor, since neighbours and villages owe one another help. He quotes Master Cheng: as steward Si had a regular salary; he declined it as too much, so the Master taught him to share it among the poor of his neighbourhood — this too was right; and Zhang Zai: from these two cases one sees how the sage used wealth. He Yan's Kong Anguo: it is the salary the rules give him, and he should not decline it.

sentences.t:
子謂仲弓曰：「
犂牛之子騂且角，
雖欲勿用，
山川其舍諸？」

morph.gloss: Zhong, the courtesy name of Guan Yiwu

sentences.l:
The Master said of Zhonggong:
“A brindled ox's calf, red and well-horned —
though men might wish not to use it,
would the hills and streams reject it?”
sentences.i: The Master said of Zhonggong: “Let the calf of a mottled ox be red, with good horns: men may not want to offer it, but will the spirits of the hills and rivers turn it away?”
sentences.n: 謂…曰 can be 'said to' or 'said of'; Zhu Xi takes it as 'of' — this is a judgement on Zhonggong, not a remark to him (此論仲弓云爾，非與仲弓言也). 犂 lí (Zhu Xi: 利之反) is 'brindled, of mixed colour'; 騂 xīng (Zhu Xi: 息營反) is red, the colour the Zhou prized in sacrificial beasts; 角 'horned' means horns well shaped and true, fit for an offering (角周正，中犧牲也). 用 'to use' is to use in sacrifice. 山川 are the spirits of the hills and streams. 舍 is shě 'to reject' (Zhu Xi: 上聲), and 諸 is 之乎 'it?'. Zhu Xi: men might not use it, but the spirits would surely not refuse it; Zhonggong's father was base and his conduct bad, and the Master uses the comparison to say that a father's badness cannot cancel a son's goodness, and a man as worthy as Zhonggong will surely be employed. He quotes Fan Zuyu: Shun had Gusou for a father and Yu had Gun, so the worthies of old did not depend on their stock; a son who can mend his father's faults and turn bad to good may be called filial. He Yan's commentary reads it the same way: though the father is not good, that does not harm the son's beauty.

sentences.t:
子曰：「回也，
其心三月不違仁，
其餘則日月至焉而已矣。」
sentences.i: The Master said: “Hui's heart can go three months without straying from humaneness. The rest get there for a day, or for a month, and no more.”
sentences.n: 三月 'three months' means a long time, Zhu Xi says; Master Cheng (quoted by Zhu Xi): three months is a season, a small turn in Heaven's course — beyond it one would be a sage. Zhu Xi: humaneness is the virtue of the heart; for the heart not to depart from it is to have no selfish desire and to keep that virtue. 日月至焉 'reach it for a day or a month' — Zhu Xi: some reach it once in a day, some once in a month; they can enter its bounds but cannot stay. 焉 'there, at it'. 而已矣 'and that is all'. Cheng again: not departing from humaneness is simply having not a hair of selfish desire; the least selfish desire is not humane. Yin Tun: this is where Yan Hui was still one step short of the sage — in the sage there is no break at all. He Yan's commentary: others reach humaneness now and then; only Hui keeps it through time without change.

sentences.t:
季康子問：「
仲由可使從政也與？」
子曰：「由也果，
於從政乎何有？」
曰：「賜也可使從政也與？」
曰：「賜也逹，
於從政乎何有？」
曰：「求也可使從政也與？」
曰：「求也藝，
於從政乎何有？」

morph.gloss: Ji, the clan name (Jisun) of the Lu house
Kang, posthumous name of Ji Kangzi
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.i: Ji Kangzi asked whether Zhong You could be given a post in the government. The Master said: “Yóu knows his own mind. What would hold him back in government?” “And Ci?” “Ci understands how things work. What would hold him back?” “And Qiu?” “Qiu can turn his hand to anything. What would hold him back?”
sentences.n: 季康子 Ji Kangzi is the head of the Ji house (2.20). 仲由 is Zilu, 賜 Zigong, 求 Ran Qiu. 從政 'to follow the business of government' — Zhu Xi: to serve as a grandee (為大夫). 與 is the question particle yú (Zhu Xi: 平聲). 果 is 'decisive, able to cut a matter short' (Zhu Xi: 有決斷; He Yan's Bao Xian: 果敢決斷); 逹, the edition's form of 達, 'to get through to the principle of things' (Zhu Xi: 通事理; Kong Anguo: 通於物理); 藝 'many talents' (Zhu Xi: 多才能). 於從政乎何有 'in government, what is there (to trouble him)?' — the 何有 of 4.13. Zhu Xi quotes Master Cheng: Kangzi asked whether the three had talent enough for government, and the Master answered that each had his strength — and not only these three: every man has one, and if his strength is used, anyone can be employed. Variant: He Yan's text writes 子曰 before the second and third answers, naming the speaker.

sentences.t:
季氏使閔子騫為費宰。
閔子騫曰：「
善為我辭焉！
如有復我者，
則吾必在汶上矣。」

morph.gloss: Ji, the clan name (Jisun) of the Lu house
clan, house (the family name as a lineage)
Min Ziqian — the disciple Min Sun
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
The Ji house would have Min Ziqian act as steward of Bi.
Min Ziqian said: “Decline it well for me!
If someone comes for me again,
then I shall surely be beyond the Wen.”
sentences.i: The Ji house wanted Min Ziqian as steward of Bi. Min Ziqian said: “Make my excuses, and make them well. If anyone comes for me a second time, I shall be over the Wen and gone.”
sentences.n: 閔子騫 Min Ziqian is the disciple Min Sun 閔損 (Zhu Xi), courtesy name Ziqian. 費 Bi, read bì (Zhu Xi: 音秘), was a town of the Ji house. 為我 'for me', 為 wèi (Zhu Xi: 去聲); 辭 'to decline'. 復 'to come again' (He Yan's Kong Anguo: 重來召我, to come summoning me again). 汶 Wen, read wèn (Zhu Xi: 音問), was a river on the border, south of Qi and north of Lu: 'on the Wen' means across it, gone to Qi. Zhu Xi: Min Ziqian would not serve the Ji as their subject, and told the messenger to excuse him well; if they summoned him again he would leave for Qi. Kong Anguo adds that the Ji were not loyal subjects of their duke and their stewards at Bi had rebelled, so they wanted a worthy man there. Zhu Xi quotes Master Cheng: of the Master's followers only a few — Min Ziqian, Master Zeng — would not serve in a grandee's house; and Xie Liangzuo at length: Min Ziqian, with the sage to lean on, saw the Ji's ill-gotten wealth and rank as dogs and swine — how could he serve them? A sage can live in a disordered state and meet bad men; below the sage, the hard man brings disaster on himself and the soft man disgrace — witness Zilu, who died a violent death, and Ran Qiu, who enriched the Ji.

sentences.t:
伯牛有疾，
子問之，
自牖執其手，
曰：「亡之，
命矣夫！
斯人也而有斯疾也！
斯人也而有斯疾也！」

morph.gloss: Bo Niu — the disciple Ran Geng

sentences.l:
Bo Niu had a sickness; the Master inquired after him.
From the window he took his hand
and said: “We are losing him —
it is fate!
This man — and to have this sickness!
This man — and to have this sickness!”
sentences.i: Bo Niu fell ill, and the Master went to see him. He took his hand through the window and said: “We are losing him. It is what Heaven has decreed. This man, of all men, to have this sickness! This man, of all men, to have this sickness!”
sentences.n: 伯牛 Bo Niu is the disciple Ran Geng 冉耕 (Zhu Xi; He Yan's Ma Rong). The sickness, Zhu Xi says, earlier scholars took to be leprosy (癩). 問 'to ask after' a sick man. 牖 yǒu is the south window: Zhu Xi explains by the rites — a sick man lies under the north window, and when his lord visits he is moved under the south one so that the lord can look at him facing south; Bo Niu's family paid Confucius this honour, and he, not daring to accept it, did not go into the room but took his hand through the window — a last farewell. He Yan's Bao Xian gives another reason: Bo Niu had a foul disease and did not wish to be seen. 亡之 is not explained by Zhu Xi; He Yan's Kong Anguo takes 亡 as wáng 'to lose' (亡，喪也): the sickness is grave, 'we are losing him'. 命 is Heaven's decree; 夫 fú closes the sigh (Zhu Xi: 音扶). Zhu Xi: such a man ought not to have had such a sickness, yet he has it — this is Heaven's decree, which shows that he had not brought it on himself by carelessness. He quotes Hou Zhongliang: Bo Niu was known for virtuous conduct, next only to Yan Hui and Min Ziqian, so the Master grieved for him most. Bao Xian: saying it twice shows the depth of his grief.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
賢哉回也！
一簞食，
一瓢飲，
在陋巷，
人不堪其憂，
回也不改其樂。
賢哉回也！」
sentences.l:
The Master said: “Worthy indeed is Hui!
One basket of rice,
one gourd of drink,
living in a poor lane —
others could not bear the misery of it;
Hui does not change his joy.
Worthy indeed is Hui!”
sentences.i: The Master said: “What a man Hui is! He lives in a back lane on one basketful of rice and one dipperful of water. Anyone else would sink under the misery of it; Hui's happiness never alters. What a man Hui is!”
sentences.n: 簞 dān is a round bamboo basket for rice; 食 is read sì, 'cooked grain, rice' (Zhu Xi: 食音嗣…飯也); 瓢 piáo is a gourd split for a dipper (Zhu Xi: 瓠也); 陋巷 is a mean, narrow lane. 樂 is lè 'joy' (Zhu Xi: 音洛). Zhu Xi: Yan Hui was this poor, yet lived calmly in it and did not let it harm his joy, so the Master said 'worthy indeed' twice in deep praise. He quotes Master Cheng: Yan Hui's joy was not joy in the basket, the gourd and the lane; he did not let poverty burden his heart and change what he delighted in; and again: the basket and the lane are not things to enjoy — he had his own joy, and the word 其 'his' should be savoured; and again: when Cheng studied under Zhou Maoshu (Zhou Dunyi), he was always told to look for the place where Zhongni and Yan Hui found joy, and what it was they enjoyed. Zhu Xi adds in his own voice that Cheng drew the bow without letting the arrow fly, meaning students to find it out for themselves; he will not presume to explain it, but a student who keeps to the teaching of 'broad in letters, restrained by the rites' (6.25, and Yan Hui's own words in Book 9) until he 'cannot stop' (欲罷不能, also Book 9) may come near it. He Yan's Kong Anguo: 簞 is a basket; Yan Yuan delighted in the Way, and did not change what he enjoyed.

sentences.t:
冉求曰：「
非不說子之道，
力不足也。」
子曰：「
力不足者，
中道而廢。
今女畫。」

morph.gloss: Ran, a surname (Ran You, Ran Qiu)

sentences.l:
Ran Qiu said: “It is not that I do not delight in your Way;
my strength is not enough.”
The Master said: “Those whose strength is not enough
break down midway on the road.
Now you draw a line.”
sentences.i: Ran Qiu said: “It is not that your Way gives me no pleasure. I just haven't the strength for it.” The Master said: “Those who truly lack the strength break down somewhere on the way. You have drawn yourself a line and stopped at it.”
sentences.n: 說 is yuè, 'to be pleased with' (Zhu Xi: 音悅); 子 'you, Master', in address. 中道 'midway', 中 zhōng — and the 道 is the plain word 'road', picking up the Master's 'Way'. 廢 'to give up, to fall'. 女 is rǔ, 'you' (Zhu Xi: 音汝). 畫 huà 'to draw a line': Zhu Xi — those whose strength is not enough want to go forward and cannot; one who draws the line can go forward and does not want to, as if drawing a line on the ground to hem himself in. He Yan's Kong Anguo: 畫 is 'to stop' — you stop yourself; it is not that your strength is exhausted. Zhu Xi quotes Hu Yin: Ran Qiu said this on hearing the Master praise Hui's unchanging joy; had he truly delighted in the Way as the mouth delights in meat, he would have spent all his strength on it, so why fear its running short? To draw a line and not go forward is to fall back day by day — which is why Ran Qiu stayed confined to his skills. Variant: He Yan's text names him 冉有 (the same man) and reads 子之道也.

sentences.t:
子謂子夏曰：「
女為君子儒，
無為小人儒。」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.i: The Master said to Zixia: “Be a scholar of the gentleman's sort, not a scholar of the petty sort.”
sentences.n: 儒 rú is the name for men of learning (Zhu Xi: 學者之稱), the word later used for the Confucians themselves. 女 is rǔ 'you'; 為 wéi 'to be'; 無 here forbids, 'do not' (= 毋). Zhu Xi quotes Master Cheng: the gentleman scholar learns for his own sake, the small man's scholar for others' eyes (為己、為人, the distinction drawn again in Book 14). He quotes Xie Liangzuo: the difference between gentleman and small man lies between what is right and what profits; and 'profit' is not only piling up goods — putting self before the common good, suiting one's own convenience, whatever harms Heaven's principle, is all profit; Zixia had learning to spare, but perhaps missed what is far and great, so the Master told him this. He Yan's commentary: the gentleman studies to make the Way plain; the small man studies to parade his name (矜其名). Variant: He Yan's text lacks 女 and prints 母 for 無, so 'be a gentleman scholar; do not be a petty scholar'.

sentences.t:
子游為武城宰。
子曰：「女得人焉耳乎？」
曰：「有澹臺滅明者，
行不由徑；
非公事，
未嘗至於偃之室也。」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
You, in Ziyou's name (言偃, courtesy name 子游)

words.reading: 澹臺滅明 tán tái miè míng

morph.gloss: Tantai Mieming — a man of Wucheng

sentences.l:
Ziyou was steward of Wucheng.
The Master said: “Have you found men there?”
He said: “There is one Tantai Mieming:
walking, he does not take side paths;
unless it is public business,
he has never once come to my room.”
sentences.i: Ziyou was governor of Wucheng. The Master said: “Have you found any good men there?” He said: “There is a man called Tantai Mieming. He keeps to the main road, never a by-path, and unless there is public business to see to he does not set foot in my quarters.”
sentences.n: 子游 Ziyou is Yan Yan 言偃 (2.7), who speaks of himself by his personal name 偃 yǎn. 武城 Wucheng was a lesser town of Lu (Zhu Xi; Bao Xian). 女 rǔ 'you'. 焉耳乎 is a run of particles: 焉 yān 'there, in it' with the softening 耳 and the question 乎; He Yan's Kong Anguo calls all of them mere particles. 澹臺滅明: surname Tantai, personal name Mieming, courtesy name Ziyu 子羽 (Zhu Xi; Bao Xian); 澹 is tán (Zhu Xi: 徒甘反). 行 is xíng 'to walk'; 徑 jìng is a small path that cuts a corner (Zhu Xi: 路之小而捷者). 公事 'public business' — Zhu Xi names the district drinking feast, the archery meeting, the reading of the laws. Zhu Xi: not taking short cuts shows that he always moved by the straight way, with no wish to snatch small gains or hurry; never coming to the steward except on business shows he kept his integrity and would not bend himself to please. He quotes Yang Shi: in government men of talent come first, so the Master asked whether Ziyou had found any; in later ages a man who would not take short cuts would be called a pedant, and one who would not call on the governor would be called stiff — who but Confucius' followers would know such a man and pick him? And Zhu Xi in his own voice: take Mieming as your model in keeping yourself, and Ziyou in choosing men. Variant: He Yan's text reads 女得人焉耳乎哉.

sentences.t:
子曰：「孟之反不伐。
奔而殿，
將入門，
策其馬，
曰：『非敢後也，
馬不進也。』」

morph.gloss: Meng Zhifan — a grandee of Lu

sentences.l:
The Master said: “Meng Zhifan does not boast.
In the rout he brought up the rear;
about to enter the gate,
he whipped his horses
and said: ‘It is not that I dared to stay behind —
the horses would not go on.’”
sentences.i: The Master said: “Meng Zhifan is not one to blow his own trumpet. When the army broke and fled he was the last man out, covering the retreat; and as he came up to the city gate he laid the whip to his horses and said: ‘Don't think I hung back out of daring — these horses wouldn't move.’”
sentences.n: 孟之反 Meng Zhifan was a grandee of Lu, personal name Ce 側 (Zhu Xi; He Yan's Kong Anguo); Zhu Xi records Hu Yin's view that he is the 孟子反 of the Zhuangzi. 伐 is 'to boast of one's merit' (Zhu Xi: 誇功也). 奔 is a rout, a defeated flight; 殿 diàn is the rear of the army (Zhu Xi: 軍後曰殿, and he marks it 去聲) — in a retreat, the place of honour and danger. 策 is a whip, here 'to whip'. Zhu Xi: when a beaten army comes home the man at the rear has the merit, so Zhifan used these words to hide it; the battle is in Duke Ai's eleventh year (484 BC), when Lu fought Qi. He quotes Xie Liangzuo: one who can hold to a heart that does not wish to rise above others will find selfish desire fading day by day and Heaven's principle growing clearer; Meng Zhifan can be taken as a model. He Yan's Ma Rong: the front of an army is called 啓 and the rear 殿; he was worthy and brave, and when people came out to greet his merit he did not want the name for himself.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
不有祝鮀之佞，
而有宋朝之美，
難乎免於今之世矣。」

morph.gloss: the invocator Tuo — a grandee of Wei
Song Zhao — Prince Zhao of Song

sentences.l:
The Master said: “Without the invocator Tuo's glibness,
and with Song Zhao's beauty,
it is hard to come through in the present age.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “If a man lacks the smooth tongue of the invocator Tuo, a handsome face like Song Zhao's will hardly save him in times like these.”
sentences.n: 祝 is an officer of the ancestral temple who speaks the prayers; 鮀 tuó (Zhu Xi: 徒何反) was a grandee of Wei, courtesy name Ziyu 子魚, known for his ready tongue (Zhu Xi; Kong Anguo, who calls 子魚 his name). 朝 Zhao was a prince of Song, famous for his good looks (Zhu Xi; Kong Anguo adds that he was given to lewdness); we read the name zhāo, as the plain reading of 朝, though cháo is also heard. 佞 nìng is a ready tongue (5.4). 難乎 'hard it is' puts the predicate first for weight. The grammar of 不有…而有… is disputed. He Yan's Kong Anguo: one ought to be glib like Tuo; if instead one has only Zhao's beauty, it is hard to escape harm in this age — so the l above. Zhu Xi glosses only: in a decayed age men love flattery and delight in good looks, and without these one can hardly escape — the Master is grieving over it; on his wording, 'without these' can take in both men, glibness and beauty together, and many read 而 here as 'and also'. Either way, it is a sour comment on the times.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
誰能出不由戸？
何莫由斯道也？」
sentences.l:
The Master said: “Who can go out except by the door?
Why does no one go by this Way?”
sentences.i: The Master said: “Nobody leaves a house except through the door. Why is it that nobody goes by this Way?”
sentences.n: 戸 is the edition's form of 戶 hù, a single-leaf door, the door of a room or house. 何莫 'why does no one…'. Zhu Xi: men cannot go out except by the door — why then do they not go by this Way? It is a cry of surprise and sorrow. He quotes Hong Xingzu: people know that to go out they must use the door, but not that to act they must follow the Way; it is not that the Way is far from men — men keep themselves far from it. He Yan's commentary: to establish oneself and succeed one must go by the Way, just as one must go in and out by the door. Variant: He Yan's text reads 誰能出不由戶者 'who is there that can go out not by the door?'.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
質勝文則野，
文勝質則史。
文質彬彬，
然後君子。」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
The Master said: “Plain stuff outweighing pattern — then a rustic;
pattern outweighing plain stuff — then a clerk.
Pattern and plain stuff mixed in even measure:
only then a gentleman.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “When the raw stuff in a man outweighs his polish he is a bumpkin; when polish outweighs the raw stuff he is a pen-pusher. Only with the two in even measure is he a gentleman.”
sentences.n: 質 zhì is the plain stuff of a man, what he is by nature and in substance; 文 is its pattern, the polish of form, learning and manner — the same 文 as 'letters' (the house word), here set against its partner. 勝 'to outdo, to overcome'. 野 'of the fields': Zhu Xi — the countryman, crude and careless (鄙略; so too He Yan's Bao Xian). 史 is the clerk who keeps documents: Zhu Xi — he hears much and is practised in affairs, but his sincerity may fall short; Bao Xian: much pattern and little stuff. 彬彬 bīn bīn, Zhu Xi says, is like 班班, things mixed and evenly balanced; Bao Xian: half pattern, half stuff. 然後 'only then'. Zhu Xi: the learner should take from what is over and add to what is lacking; when his virtue is complete, the balance comes without his aiming at it. He quotes Yang Shi: pattern and stuff must not overcome each other; still, stuff outweighing pattern is like sweetness, which can take seasoning, or white, which can take colour; but pattern that destroys the stuff has lost the root, and then where would the pattern be laid on? So 'rather rustic than clerk'.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
人之生也直，
罔之生也幸而免。」
sentences.l:
The Master said: “Man's living is straightness;
the crooked man's living is luck, a narrow escape.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “Men live by being straight. When a crooked man lives, he has had a lucky escape.”
sentences.n: 生 'to be born, to live'; 直 'straight, upright'; 罔 wǎng is 'crooked, false' — Master Cheng (quoted by Zhu Xi): the principle of life is straight in its root; 罔 is not straight, and if such a man lives too, he has escaped by luck. He Yan's Ma Rong: a man lives in the world and comes to a good end by the way of straightness; Bao Xian takes 罔 as 'to deceive' (誣), one who defames the straight Way. 幸 'by luck'; 免 'to escape (harm)'. The two 之…也 clauses are parallel: 'as for X's living…'.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
知之者不如好之者，
好之者不如樂之者。」
sentences.l:
The Master said: “One who knows it is no match for one who loves it;
one who loves it is no match for one who rejoices in it.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “Knowing it is not as good as loving it, and loving it not as good as rejoicing in it.”
sentences.n: 之 'it' is left unnamed; Zhu Xi's Yin Tun makes it the Way: knowing it is knowing that there is this Way; loving it is loving it without yet having got it; delighting in it is having got something and delighting in that. 好 hào 'to love' (Zhu Xi: 去聲); 樂 lè 'to delight in' (Zhu Xi: 音洛). 不如 'not as good as'. Zhu Xi also quotes Zhang Shi: take the five grains — the knower knows they can be eaten; the lover eats and relishes them; the delighter relishes them and is full; to know and not love is knowing that has not arrived; to love and not delight is loving that has not arrived — which is why the learners of old drove themselves on without rest. He Yan's Bao Xian says the same of learning: knowing it is less earnest (篤) than loving it, loving it less deep (深) than delighting in it. Variant: He Yan's text begins 知者不如好之者 'the knower is not equal to one who loves it', though Bao Xian's comment has 知之者.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
中人以上，
可以語上也；
中人以下，
不可以語上也。」
sentences.i: The Master said: “To those of middling gifts and above one may speak of the higher matters. To those of middling gifts and below one may not.”
sentences.n: 中人 'a man in the middle', of ordinary gifts. 以上, 以下 'and above', 'and below'; Zhu Xi reads the first 上 shǎng (以上之上上聲) as the verb-like 'upwards', a reading modern practice does not keep — we give shàng. 語 is yù, 'to tell, to instruct' (Zhu Xi: 去聲；語，告也), and the second 上 is 'what is high'. Zhu Xi: one who teaches should speak to each according to his height, so that the words go in easily and there is no fault of skipping stages. He quotes Zhang Shi: the sage's Way is one in its fine and coarse parts, but in teaching it must follow each man's material; tell a man below the middle something too high, all at once, and not only will it not go in, he will fancy himself past the stages and lose touch with himself, and end at the bottom after all — so speak to him at the level he can reach, and he will ask closely and think of what is near, and rise by degrees. He Yan's Wang Su: 'the higher' means what the highest wise know; the middling man is named on both sides because he can go up or down.

sentences.t:
樊遲問知。
子曰：「
務民之義，
敬鬼神而遠之，
可謂知矣。」
問仁。
曰：「仁者先難而後獲，
可謂仁矣。」

morph.gloss: Chi, from Fan Xu's courtesy name 子遲

sentences.l:
Fan Chi asked about wisdom.
The Master said: “To devote oneself to what is right for the people,
to revere ghosts and spirits and keep them far off —
this can be called wisdom.”
He asked about humaneness.
He said: “The humane man puts the hard part first and the gain last —
this can be called humaneness.”
sentences.i: Fan Chi asked what wisdom is. The Master said: “To give yourself to what is right among men, and to honour the ghosts and spirits but hold them at arm's length — that may be called wisdom.” He asked about humaneness. The Master said: “The humane man takes on the hard work first and thinks of the reward afterwards. That may be called humaneness.”
sentences.n: 樊遲 Fan Chi (2.5). 知 is zhì, 'wisdom' (Zhu Xi: 去聲). 務 'to give one's effort to'. 民之義: Zhu Xi takes 民 as simply 'men' (民亦人也) — to spend one's strength on what is fitting in the human way and not be led astray by spirits that cannot be known is the business of the wise; He Yan's Wang Su reads it as the ruler's task, 'to work at what leads the people to what is right'. 遠 'to keep at a distance': Zhu Xi reads the verb yuàn (遠皆去聲), a reading modern practice does not keep; we give yuǎn. 鬼神 are the spirits of the dead and other spirits. 先難而後獲: Zhu Xi — to put first what is hard in the task and to put last the result it earns is the heart of the humane; he adds that the Master must have said it because of some failing in Fan Chi. 獲 huò 'to get, gain'. He quotes Master Cheng: many believe in spirits, which is delusion, and those who do not believe cannot revere them; to revere them and keep them at a distance can be called wise; and again: 'the hard part first' is overcoming oneself (克己) — putting the hard first and not reckoning the gain is humane. And Lü Dalin: make the urgent business the first business and do not seek what is hard to know; do what you know with all your strength, and do not shrink from what is hard to do. He Yan's Bao Xian: revere the spirits and do not presume on them; Kong Anguo: first the toil, then the reward. Variant: He Yan's text reads 問仁子曰.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
知者樂水，
仁者樂山。
知者動，
仁者静。
知者樂，
仁者壽。」
sentences.i: The Master said: “The wise are drawn to water, the humane to hills. The wise are always on the move, the humane keep still. The wise have their joy, the humane their length of days.”
sentences.n: 知者 'the wise man', 知 zhì (Zhu Xi: 去聲). 樂 is read three ways in the Analects; Zhu Xi reads the first two here yào 'to delight in, to have a liking for' (五教反, 樂，喜好也) and the last lè 'to be joyful' (音洛); modern practice keeps both readings. 静 is the edition's form of 靜 jìng 'still'; 壽 shòu 'long life'. Zhu Xi: the wise man sees through the principle of affairs and flows round them without check, like water, so he takes to water; the humane man rests in what is right and is solid and unmoving, like a mountain, so he takes to mountains. Moving and still describe their substance, joy and long life their results: moving without being bound, he is joyful; still and constant, he lives long. He quotes Master Cheng: none but one who embodied humaneness and wisdom deeply could describe them so. He Yan's Bao Xian: the wise man delights to use his talent and wisdom to order the world, as water flows on and does not stop; an unattributed comment there: the humane man delights to be like a mountain, settled, firm, unmoving, while all things grow on it; Kong Anguo: he is still because he has no desires; Bao Xian: his nature is still, so he lives long.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
齊一變，
至於魯；
魯一變，
至於道。」
sentences.l:
The Master said: “Qi, changing once, would reach Lu;
Lu, changing once, would reach the Way.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “Qi needs one change to be where Lu is; Lu needs one change to be where the Way is.”
sentences.n: 齊 Qi and 魯 Lu were neighbouring states, Lu the Master's own. 變 'to change'. Zhu Xi: in the Master's time Qi's customs were set on quick gain and success and fond of boasting and deceit, the habits left over from its hegemon's government; Lu still valued the rites and teaching and prized good faith and what is right, and kept something of the manner of the former kings, though, its men gone, its government had lapsed. 道 is the Way of the former kings. So the two states, differing in their governments and customs, would find it easier or harder to change toward the Way. He quotes Master Cheng: in the Master's day Qi was strong and Lu weak, and who would not have thought Qi the better? But Lu still kept the institutions of the Duke of Zhou, while Qi, since Duke Huan's hegemony, had gone over to a government of shortcuts and results, and the laws left by the Taigong were all changed; so Qi needed one change to reach Lu, and Lu needed only to restore what had fallen to reach the Way of the former kings. Zhu Xi adds in his own voice that only the Master could have changed the two, and he was never given the trial. He Yan's Bao Xian: both kept something of the influence of the Taigong and the Duke of Zhou; under an enlightened ruler, Qi could be made like Lu and Lu like the time when the great Way prevailed.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
觚不觚，
觚哉！觚哉！」
sentences.l:
The Master said: “A gu not shaped as a gu —
a gu, that! A gu, that!”
sentences.i: The Master said: “A gu with no corners to it — some gu! Some gu!”
sentences.n: 觚 gū (Zhu Xi: 音孤) is a cornered thing: Zhu Xi says the word means a corner or ridge (稜), and that some take it as a wine vessel, some as a wooden writing tablet — either way, a thing with corners. 不觚 'not cornered': Zhu Xi — people of the time had lost its proper form and no longer made it with corners; 'a gu indeed!' says it can no longer be called a gu. He quotes Master Cheng: a gu that loses its form is not a gu; take one vessel, and all things under heaven are the same — a ruler who loses the way of a ruler is no ruler, a minister who loses a minister's office fills an empty place; and Fan Zuyu: a man who is not humane is no man, a state not governed is no state. He Yan's Ma Rong: the gu is a ritual vessel — a one-sheng cup is a 爵, a two-sheng one a 觚; an unattributed comment there: the cry means it is not a gu, a figure for government that has not got its Way and so achieves nothing.

sentences.t:
宰我問曰：「仁者，
雖告之曰：『井有仁焉。』
其從之也？」
子曰：「何為其然也？
君子可逝也，
不可陷也；
可欺也，
不可罔也。」

morph.gloss: a steward, the chief officer of a noble house
a man (仁 read as 人)
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
Zai Wo asked, saying: “The humane man — even if told,
‘There is a man in the well,’
would he follow him in?”
The Master said: “Why would it be so?
The gentleman can be sent to go there,
but cannot be trapped;
he can be tricked,
but cannot be befuddled.”
sentences.i: Zai Wo asked: “Suppose a humane man were told that someone had fallen down a well. Would he climb down after him?” The Master said: “Why should he? A gentleman can be made to go to the well, but not to throw himself in; he can be taken in by a plausible story, but not fooled by an absurd one.”
sentences.n: 宰我 Zai Wo is Zai Yu (3.21, 5.9). 告 gào 'to tell'. 井有仁焉: Zhu Xi follows Liu Mianzhi (劉聘君), who says the 仁 of 有仁 should be 人 'a man', and so we translate; the text keeps 仁 as printed, and He Yan's Kong Anguo reads it as it stands — 'a humane man has fallen into the well' (有仁人墮井). 從 cóng 'to follow' — Zhu Xi: to follow him into the well to save him. 何為 'for what?', 為 wèi. 逝 shì, 'to go' — Zhu Xi: to be sent to go and save him; 陷 xiàn 'to be trapped', made to fall into the well; 欺 qī 'to deceive' with what is possible in principle; 罔 wǎng 'to befuddle' with what is impossible. Zhu Xi: Zai Wo's faith in the Way was not firm, and he worried that the humane would be ruined by their humaneness, hence the question; but a man on the well's rim can save the man in it, while one who follows him in can save nobody — this is plain to anyone, and the humane man, however eager to save others and careless of himself, would not be so foolish. Kong Anguo: Zai Wo held that the humane must save men from danger, and was testing how far the humane man's concern would go; Bao Xian: he can be made to go and look, but will not throw himself in; Ma Rong: he can be made to go, but cannot be fooled into jumping. Variant: He Yan's text reads 井有仁者焉 'there is a humane man in the well'.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
君子博學於文，
約之以禮，
亦可以弗畔矣夫！」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
The Master said: “The gentleman, learning broadly in letters
and drawing it in by the rites,
can also keep from turning away!”
sentences.i: The Master said: “Let a gentleman learn widely in the written tradition and gather it in by the rites, and he too can keep from turning his back on the Way.”
sentences.n: 博 'broad, wide'; 文 'letters', the written tradition. 約 yuē is 'to bind, to draw together', Zhu Xi: 要也 'to bring to the essential'. 畔 pàn = 背 'to turn one's back on' (Zhu Xi), understood: the Way; He Yan's Zheng Xuan: 弗畔 is not to go against the Way. 亦 'also, after all'. 夫 is the closing exclamation fú (Zhu Xi: 音扶). Zhu Xi: the gentleman wants his learning broad, so there is nothing in letters he does not look into; he wants his holding fast to be essential, so in every movement he keeps the rites; so he can keep from turning away from the Way. He quotes Master Cheng: broad learning in letters without the restraint of the rites must end in a shapeless sprawl; to learn broadly and also keep the rites and go by rule — that too can keep one from turning from the Way. The whole saying comes back at 12.15.

sentences.t:
子見南子，
子路不説。
夫子矢之曰：「
予所否者，
天厭之！
天厭之！」

morph.gloss: Nanzi — the wife of Duke Ling of Wei
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)

sentences.l:
The Master saw Nanzi.
Zilu was not pleased.
The Master swore it, saying:
“If I did wrong in it,
may Heaven cast me off!
May Heaven cast me off!”
sentences.i: The Master had an audience with Nanzi, and Zilu was displeased. The Master swore to him: “If I did what I should not have, let Heaven cast me off! Let Heaven cast me off!”
sentences.n: 南子 Nanzi was the wife of Duke Ling of Wei 衛靈公, of loose conduct (Zhu Xi). Zhu Xi: when Confucius came to Wei, Nanzi asked to see him; he declined, and only when he could not avoid it went — for in antiquity one who took office in a state had a rite of presenting himself to its ruler's consort; Zilu thought it a disgrace that the Master should see so lewd a woman, and was displeased. 説 is the edition's form of 說, read yuè 'pleased' (Zhu Xi: 音悅). 矢 shǐ is 'to swear' (Zhu Xi: 誓也). 所…者 is the form of an oath, 'if I…' — Zhu Xi compares the Zuo zhuan's 所不與崔慶者 'if I do not side with Cui and Qing…'. 否 fǒu (Zhu Xi: 方九反) is 'what is not so': not in accord with the rites, not by the Way. 厭 yàn is 'to cast off, reject utterly' (Zhu Xi: 棄絕也). 予 yú 'I'. Zhu Xi: the sage, whose Way is great and virtue whole, has nothing he must do and nothing he must not (無可不可); in seeing a bad person he takes it that if there is a rite for it on his side, her wrongdoing is no concern of his — but how could Zilu fathom that? So he swore it twice over, wanting Zilu to trust him for now and think it through. He Yan's Kong Anguo reports a different account — that the Master saw her hoping through her to persuade Duke Ling to govern well, and swore because Zilu was displeased — and himself calls the oath 'of doubtful sense'.

sentences.t:
子曰：「
中庸之為德也，
其至矣乎！
民鮮久矣。」
sentences.l:
The Master said: “The mean-and-constant as a virtue —
is it not the utmost!
The people have long been short of it.”
sentences.i: The Master said: “The everyday middle path is the highest of virtues; and it is long since many people had it.”
sentences.n: 中庸 is two words: Zhu Xi — 中 is the name for 'neither too much nor too little' (無過無不及), 庸 is 'ordinary, constant' (平常); He Yan's commentary: 庸 is 'constant', and 中庸 the virtue of balance and harmony that can always be practised. Zhu Xi quotes Master Cheng: what does not lean is 中, what does not change is 庸; 中 is the right Way of the world, 庸 its fixed principle. The phrase gives its name to the Zhongyong (Doctrine of the Mean), a chapter of the Liji which Zhu Xi made one of the Four Books. 之為德也 'its being a virtue'. 其至矣乎 'surely it is the utmost!'. 鮮 xiǎn 'few, rare' (Zhu Xi: 上聲；少也). Zhu Xi: the people have been short of this virtue for a long time now; Cheng: since the teaching of the age declined, the people have not been roused to practise it. He Yan's commentary: the world is disordered, the Way of the former kings has fallen, and the people have long been unable to practise it — not only now.

sentences.t:
子貢曰：「
如有博施於民而能濟衆，
何如？可謂仁乎？」
子曰：「
何事於仁！
必也聖乎？
堯舜其猶病諸！」

morph.gloss: the Master (alone as speaker, always Confucius)
to be like, to come up to

sentences.l:
Zigong said: “If there were one who bestowed broadly on the people
and could relieve the multitude —
what of him? Could he be called humane?”
The Master said: “Why only humaneness!
Surely it would take a sage?
Even Yao and Shun still felt themselves short in this.”
sentences.i: Zigong said: “What would you say of a man who spread his bounty over all the people and brought relief to the whole multitude? Could he be called humane?” The Master said: “Humane? That goes beyond humaneness — would it not take a sage? Even Yao and Shun felt they fell short in this.”
sentences.n: 博 'broad'; 施 'to bestow, give out' — Zhu Xi reads it shì (施去聲), a reading modern practice does not keep; we give shī. 濟 jì 'to bring across, to relieve'; 衆 (the edition's form) 'the many'. 何如 'what of…?' (1.15). 何事於仁 — Zhu Xi: 'how would it stop at humaneness?' (何止於仁). 聖 shèng is a sage: Zhu Xi — 仁 speaks of a principle that runs through high and low, 聖 of a standing, the name for reaching the very top. 必也聖乎 'surely it would take a sage?' — 乎, Zhu Xi says, is a word of doubt, not yet settled (疑而未定之辭). 堯 Yao and 舜 Shun are the sage kings of high antiquity. 病 'to be troubled by, to find oneself short': Zhu Xi — the heart feels itself lacking; even Yao and Shun, sages, still felt they fell short here; 諸 is 之乎. Zhu Xi: to look for humaneness this way makes it ever harder and ever farther off. He Yan's Kong Anguo: if one could spread kindness widely and save the people from distress, even Yao and Shun, perfect sages, would find it hard. Variant: He Yan's text reads 如能博施於民而能濟衆者 'if one could bestow broadly on the people and relieve the many'.

sentences.t:
夫仁者，
己欲立而立人，
己欲達而達人。
sentences.i: Wanting firm footing for himself, the humane man gives others firm footing; wanting to make his own way through, he clears a way for others.
sentences.n: The print has 已欲立而立人巳欲達, a misprint for 己欲立而立人己欲達, corrected here. The copy confuses 己 'oneself', 已 'to stop' and 巳 throughout (as at 4.14 and 5.15); Master Cheng, quoted in Zhu Xi's comment on the passage, gives the line with 己 both times (and Zhu Xi's own 以己及人 has 己), the first collation witness (Ruan's 1816 text) reads 己 (He Yan's text has the same 已…巳 as the print), and 'oneself' is the only sense the line allows. 夫 fú opens a general statement, 'now' (Zhu Xi: 音扶). The Master's answer runs on from the last unit; the commentary has broken it. 立 'to stand, to be established'; 達 dá 'to get through, to make one's way' — the same verbs used first of oneself, then (立人, 達人) causatively of others. Zhu Xi: to reach out from oneself to others is the heart of the humane man; here one can see Heaven's principle flowing round without a break, and nothing pictures the substance of humaneness more closely than this.

sentences.t:
能近取譬，
可謂仁之方也巳。

morph.gloss: and that is all (巳 = 已)

sentences.l:
To be able to take one's comparison from near at hand —
this may be called the means to humaneness, and that is all.
sentences.i: To be able to judge others by what lies nearest — oneself: that is the way to set about humaneness.
sentences.n: 譬 pì is 'a comparison' (Zhu Xi: 喻也); 方 is 'a method, a means' (Zhu Xi: 術也; He Yan's Kong Anguo: 道也). 也巳 is 也已 'and that is all': 巳 is the edition's form here (as at 5.26), read yǐ. Zhu Xi: take the comparison from what is near, from oneself: by what one wants oneself one knows that others want the same, then extend what they want to them — this is the work of 恕 'fellow-feeling' (the 恕 of 4.15) and the method of humaneness; work at it, and one can overcome the selfishness of one's desires and make whole the impartiality of Heaven's principle. He quotes Master Cheng: the medical books call numbness of hands and feet 'not humane' (不仁), which describes humaneness best; the humane man takes heaven, earth and the myriad things as one body with himself, so nothing is not himself; if things do not belong to oneself they are no concern of one's own, as numb limbs are not reached by one's breath. Cheng again: the Analects twice says that 'even Yao and Shun found it hard' (here and in Book 14, of 修己以安百姓); the sage wishes to give broadly, but in his time only the fifty-year-olds wore silk and the seventy-year-olds ate meat; he wishes to save the many, but his rule reached no further than the nine provinces. And Lü Dalin: Zigong was set on humaneness, but chased the high and far and did not know the method; the Master taught him to take it from himself, which is near and can be entered. Kong Anguo: he explains the humane man's conduct again for Zigong — just take the comparison from oneself, and what one does not want, do not do to others.
